title: Disadvantages (DAs)
subtitle: Negative Fundamentals · Mission 06
tagline: The AFF's plan sounds nice. You prove it {{amber:causes something worse}}. Meet the {{amber:DA}} — the Negative's most feared weapon — and its three parts.

slides.headline: 🐶 THE PUPPY PROBLEM
body: You really want a puppy. You've made your case: *"It'll be fun. I'll take care of it. Please."* 🥺
Your parents say: *"If we get a puppy, {{amber:nobody will walk it}}, {{amber:it'll destroy the furniture}}, and {{amber:we'll have to move}} because of the pet deposit."*
They didn't say "no." They didn't attack your plan directly. They ran a {{amber:Disadvantage}} — a chain of bad side effects that make your plan a {{amber:bad idea}} even if it works. 💥
The Negative team does this in every round. It's their favorite weapon. Today: {{amber:learn to build one}}.

items.label: Define the {{amber:Disadvantage}} and why it's the Neg's top weapon
Master the three parts: {{amber:Uniqueness · Link · Impact}}
Diagnose a broken DA using {{amber:Disad Dan}} on the cliff

slides.definition: A {{amber:Disadvantage}} (DA) is the Negative's most common {{amber:off-case}} attack. It says: *"Sure, the plan might sound fine — but it causes {{amber:this terrible side effect}} that outweighs anything good."* 💥
slides.plainWords: You don't argue the plan won't work. You argue that it works AND causes something worse. Net bad.
slides.analogy: Think of it like {{amber:medicine}}. 💊 The plan cures the headache — sure. But it also gives you a horrible stomachache. If the stomachache is worse than the headache, you {{amber:don't take the medicine}}. That's the whole game.

slides.headline: U-L-I: THE THREE PARTS OF A DA
slides.intro: Every winning Disadvantage has {{amber:three parts}} — in order. Miss one and the DA falls apart. Learn to say the names out loud: {{amber:Uniqueness → Link → Impact}}.

cards.name: U — UNIQUENESS
cards.description: Things are {{amber:okay right now}}. The disaster hasn't happened yet. This proves the plan is what changes things — not something else already going on.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: *"The economy is stable right now — steady growth, low unemployment."* Uniqueness locked in. ✅

cards.name: L — LINK
cards.description: The {{amber:plan specifically}} causes the problem. Not "stuff in general" — {{amber:this plan}} pushes the domino. Point to the exact action.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: *"Their plan spends $2 trillion — that shock crashes the stable economy."* Link locked in. 🔗

cards.name: I — IMPACT
cards.description: The disaster the plan {{amber:causes}}. Big, scary, real. This is what makes the judge care. Higher magnitude = stronger DA.

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: *"Recession costs 3 million jobs and drags the world into economic crisis."* Impact locked in. 💥

slides.headline: 🧍 MEET DISAD DAN
slides.intro: Here's the trick every good Neg debater knows: the three parts of a DA are just {{amber:Disad Dan on a cliff}}. He can only be pushed off if he's {{amber:right on the edge}}. Diagnose your DA before you run it — is Dan in the right spot?

rows.name: 🏔️ Dan's cliff = Uniqueness
rows.description: Dan has to be standing {{amber:right on the edge}} — safe *for now*, but one push away from falling. That's Uniqueness. Things are okay {{amber:right now}}, but fragile.

counter.label: In a round
counter.text: *"The economy is stable — but growth is slow and one shock could tip it."* Dan's on the edge. 🧍

rows.name: 🤖 The push = Link
rows.description: The AFF plan is the {{amber:hand that pushes Dan}}. You have to prove {{amber:this plan}} — not some other plan, not "policy in general" — is what shoves him.

counter.label: In a round
counter.text: *"Their plan spends $2T — that's the push. No other bill on the table does that."* 🤖

rows.name: 💥 The fall = Impact
rows.description: Dan falls into disaster. This is the {{amber:big scary thing}} the judge votes on. Bigger fall = stronger DA.

counter.label: In a round
counter.text: *"He falls into a recession. 3 million jobs lost. Global crisis."* 💥

rows.name: ⚠️ Diagnose before you run it
rows.description: If Dan is {{amber:too far from the edge}} → your push doesn't matter (no real Uniqueness). If Dan is {{amber:already falling}} → the plan isn't the cause (Aff will say *"it's happening anyway"*). Only {{amber:right on the edge}} = a DA that wins.

counter.label: Pro tip
counter.text: *"Before you read the DA, ask: is Dan on the edge? If he's already falling, {{amber:pick a different DA}}."*

prompt.label: PARTS MATCH
prompt.scenario: A Neg team is running an *"Economy DA"* against a spending plan. Three sentences from their speech are below. Match each one to the part of the DA it's doing.
prompt.question: Drag each sentence on the left to the right {{amber:part of the DA}} on the right.

items.text: *"Their plan spends two trillion dollars — that shock crashes the market."*
*"A recession would cost three million jobs and trigger a global crisis."*
*"The economy is stable right now — steady growth, low unemployment."*
🧊 UNIQUENESS — things are OK right now

correct.title: ✓ THREE PARTS LOCKED IN
body: That's the DA architecture. {{cyan:Uniqueness}} sets the scene (*things are OK*). {{amber:Link}} is the plan-specific push (*this plan breaks it*). {{amber:Impact}} is the disaster (*here's why the judge should care*). Every DA needs all three. 🎯
correct.followup: **Pro move:** In a speech, say the words out loud in order: *"Uniqueness — [scene]. Link — [plan causes]. Impact — [disaster]."* The judge is listening for those three words.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ RESHUFFLE
body: Quick test: {{cyan:Uniqueness}} = *"things are okay right now."* {{amber:Link}} = *"the plan specifically breaks it."* {{amber:Impact}} = *"here's the disaster."* Re-read each sentence and ask which of the three questions it's answering.

prompt.label: THE CLIMATE TRAP
prompt.scenario:
A Neg team wants to run *"The plan causes climate change"* as a Disadvantage. But climate change is {{amber:already happening}} — scientists say the planet is already warming.

Why is this DA broken?
prompt.question: Which part of the DA falls apart when the impact is {{amber:already happening}}?

options.text: The Link — you can't link a plan to climate change
The Uniqueness — if it's already happening, you can't blame the plan
The Impact — climate change isn't a big enough impact
Nothing is broken — it's still a good DA

correct.title: ✓ CAUGHT THE TRAP
body: Exactly. {{cyan:Uniqueness}} means *the disaster hasn't happened yet*. If climate change is {{amber:already underway}}, the Aff will just say: *"That's happening anyway — it's not our plan's fault."* {{amber:Disad Dan is already falling}} — no push needed. 🧍‍♂️💨
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** Before you run any DA, check Uniqueness first. If the disaster is already happening, {{amber:pick a different DA}}. Climate change makes a great {{amber:Impact}} — but only if you can prove the plan {{amber:uniquely}} makes it worse.

a.title: ✕ LINK ISN'T THE PROBLEM
body: Actually, you probably {{amber:can}} link a plan to climate change (e.g. "the plan increases emissions"). The problem is different: even if you link it, climate change is already happening, so the Aff will say *"that's happening anyway."* That's a {{amber:Uniqueness}} problem, not a Link one.

c.title: ✕ IMPACT IS FINE
body: Climate change is a {{amber:huge}} impact — one of the biggest in debate. That's not the issue. The issue is {{cyan:Uniqueness}}: if it's already happening, you can't say the {{amber:plan}} is what causes it.

d.title: ✕ IT'S BROKEN
body: The Aff will crush this DA with one sentence: *"Climate change is happening anyway — the Neg needs to prove {{amber:our plan uniquely makes it worse}}."* Without Uniqueness, the DA is dead.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:B — Uniqueness}}. If the disaster is already happening, you can't blame the plan. Disad Dan is already falling.

prompt.label: DA TRIAGE
prompt.scenario: You're building a *"Federal Spending DA"* against an infrastructure plan. Six lines from your notes are jumbled. Sort each one into {{cyan:UNIQUENESS}}, {{amber:LINK}}, or {{amber:IMPACT}}.
prompt.question: Drop each line into the right bin.

cards.text: *"The federal deficit is currently manageable — Congress just passed a stable budget."*
*"The plan adds $1.5 trillion in new spending on top of the existing deficit."*
*"A debt crisis would collapse the dollar and trigger a global depression."*
*"The plan's specific funding mechanism requires new Treasury bonds."*
*"Investor confidence in U.S. debt is high right now."*
*"Global depressions kill millions through poverty, unrest, and collapsed healthcare."*

correct.title: ✓ TRIAGE COMPLETE
body: That's how a Neg debater preps a DA. Group your notes by part. {{cyan:Uniqueness}} lines = *right now*. {{amber:Link}} lines = *this plan specifically*. {{amber:Impact}} lines = *the disaster*.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** If any bin is {{amber:empty}}, your DA has a hole. No Uniqueness card? The Aff says *"already happening."* No Link card? The Aff says *"not our plan."* No Impact card? The judge says *"so what?"* Build all three or {{amber:the DA loses}}.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ RE-TRIAGE
body: Litmus test: is the sentence about {{cyan:how things are now}} → **Uniqueness**. About {{amber:the plan doing something specific}} → **Link**. About {{amber:the disaster that follows}} → **Impact**.

prompt.label: DIAGNOSE DAN
prompt.scenario: Three Neg teams are pitching Disadvantages. In each case, {{amber:Disad Dan}} is in a different spot. Which DA is actually going to win?
prompt.question: Pick the DA where Disad Dan is {{amber:right on the edge}}.

options.text: *"The plan causes climate change."* — Dan is already falling (climate change is already happening)
*"The plan causes a recession."* — Dan is on the edge (economy is stable but fragile, plan is the push)
*"The plan makes politicians unpopular."* — Dan is too far from the edge (politicians are already unpopular)
*"The plan will end all life on Earth eventually."* — Dan is nowhere near the cliff (no realistic link)

correct.title: ✓ DIAGNOSIS CORRECT
body: That's the winning DA. {{amber:Uniqueness}} = economy is stable *but fragile*. {{amber:Link}} = this plan's spending is the push. {{amber:Impact}} = recession. All three parts hold. Dan gets shoved off the cliff. 💥
correct.followup: **Big lesson:** A DA can have an amazing Impact and still lose if Dan is {{amber:already falling}} or {{amber:too far from the edge}}. Diagnose Dan {{amber:before}} you commit to running the DA.

a.title: ✕ DAN'S ALREADY FALLING
body: Climate change is already happening — Dan's mid-fall. Aff says *"happening anyway."* No {{amber:Uniqueness}} = broken DA. Try again.

c.title: ✕ DAN'S TOO FAR BACK
body: If politicians are {{amber:already}} unpopular, the plan can't make them *more* unpopular in a way that matters. No {{amber:Uniqueness}} = the push doesn't do anything.

d.title: ✕ DAN'S IN THE PARKING LOT
body: Huge impact, but the {{amber:Link}} is a fantasy — no real chain from "the plan" to "end of all life." Judges will laugh this out of the room. The best DA has a {{amber:believable}} link.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:B}}. The recession DA has all three parts: stable-but-fragile Uniqueness, plan-specific Link, and a real Impact. Dan is right on the edge.

prompt.label: BIG IDEA CHECK
prompt.question: 🎯 The DA is like {{amber:medicine that cures your headache but gives you a stomachache}}. What does this analogy actually teach you about running a DA?

options.text: You don't have to prove the plan fails — you just have to prove the {{amber:side effects}} are worse than the benefits
You have to prove the plan doesn't do anything good at all
The judge always votes for the team with the smaller impact
DAs only work if the plan is about medicine or health

correct.title: ✓ THAT'S THE WHOLE GAME
body: Exactly. The DA doesn't say *"the plan won't work."* It says *"the plan works AND causes something worse."* {{amber:Net bad}}. The Aff can prove their whole case and {{amber:still lose}} because the DA outweighs. 💊
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** This is why the DA is the Neg's favorite weapon. It doesn't fight the Aff head-on — it makes the plan {{amber:net bad}}. Combine it with the {{amber:impact calculus}} you learned last mission and you have a knockout.

b.title: ✕ TOO STRONG
body: You don't need to prove the plan does *nothing* — that's an on-case attack. The DA {{amber:concedes}} the plan does something and argues the {{amber:side effects}} are worse.

c.title: ✕ BACKWARDS
body: The judge votes for the team whose impacts {{amber:outweigh}} — usually the {{amber:bigger}} and more likely impact wins. The DA is trying to make the Neg's impact *bigger* than the Aff's.

d.title: ✕ IT'S AN ANALOGY
body: The medicine is just a metaphor. DAs work on {{amber:any}} kind of plan — spending, foreign policy, education, anything. The point is *side effects worse than the fix*.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:A}}. A DA doesn't kill the plan by proving it fails — it kills the plan by proving the {{amber:side effects outweigh}} the benefits. Net bad.

slides.headline: DA LOCKED IN 💥
slides.subtext: You've got the DA — the Negative's favorite weapon. Three parts: {{cyan:Uniqueness}} (things are OK right now), {{amber:Link}} (the plan specifically breaks it), {{amber:Impact}} (disaster). Diagnose {{amber:Disad Dan}} on the cliff before every DA. If he's on the edge, push. If he's already falling or too far back — pick a different DA.
